title: Open plan offices are terrible for innovation and productivity
summary: Summarises three studies suggesting open-plan offices reduce face-to-face collaboration, increase distraction, and that alternating group and solo work beats constant collaboration.

assertions.quote: the amount of collaboration in open-plan offices was actually lower than when people had their own individual space

verdicts.note: The Bernstein and Turban field study at two Fortune 500 firms found face-to-face interaction fell by roughly seventy percent after the switch; it is two sites but with objective sensor data.

Two Fortune 500 headquarters moved from cubicles to open floors; wearable badges and server logs showed face-to-face time fell 72% (5.8 to 1.7 h per person per day) at the first firm and 67-71% at the second, while emails sent rose 56%, received 20-50% and IM messages 67%; quasi-experiment without a control group, 52 and 100 participants.

assertions.quote: people in open plan offices complained that they were significantly more prone to distraction

verdicts.note: Large occupant surveys such as Kim and de Dear find open-plan workers less satisfied, especially on noise and privacy, with no offsetting gain in ease of interaction.

Not measured in the study; the paper's review cites prior workplace design research finding open offices reduce focus and psychological privacy, and the discussion notes employees isolating themselves with large headphones, so support here is second-hand.

assertions.quote: people were both collaborating for part of the time and then had time to work individually this gave the high performers the chance

verdicts.note: The Bernstein, Shore and Lazer intermittent-collaboration experiment found this pattern, though on abstract problem-solving tasks rather than software work.

Cites Bernstein, Shore and Lazer finding that intermittent rather than constant social influence produced the best performance in collective problem solving, alongside the paper's own result that constant openness cut face-to-face interaction about 70%; the supporting study is a cited working paper, not this paper's data.
